Cubism. An early twentieth-century revolutionary art movement that deconstructed forms into geometric shapes and multiple viewpoints, showing objects from many different angles all at once on a flat surface. Pioneered by Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque around nineteen seven to nineteen fourteen, Cubism rejected realistic perspective entirely and fundamentally changed how artists and viewers understood representation and abstraction.

Picasso's Les Demoiselles d'Avignon from nineteen seven is often cited as the first Cubist painting. It features distorted female figures fragmented across an angular, disorienting composition that shocked viewers at the time. The movement then split into two main phases. Analytical Cubism, from nineteen eight to nineteen twelve, pushed fragmentation so far it approached near-abstraction, with muted earth tones and forms that were barely legible. Then came Synthetic Cubism, from nineteen twelve to nineteen fourteen, which reintroduced color and introduced collage elements, papier collé.

The key technical innovation was showing multiple perspectives of an object simultaneously. A guitar might be seen from the front, the side, and from inside all at once, collapsing the traditional single-point perspective that had dominated European art for centuries.

Juan Gris refined Cubism into a more geometric and almost mathematical formalism, prioritizing grid structures and clarity over the expressionism of Braque and Picasso. The movement was exhibited prominently at the nineteen eleven Salon d'Automne in Paris and again at the nineteen thirteen Armory Show in New York, where it shocked conservative audiences and scandalized the press.

Cubism's influence spread rapidly. It rippled into Dada, Constructivism, and later movements, profoundly shaping architecture, design, and sculpture for decades to come.
